title: Senate Passes Bipartisan Permitting Overhaul 62-33; Data Centers Would Pay Their Own Power Costs
excerpt: The U.S. Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill Thursday to speed up federal approval of energy projects, including power plants, transmission lines and data…
content:
The U.S. Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill Thursday to speed up federal approval of energy projects, including power plants, transmission lines and data centers, and to make data centers pay for the electricity grid upgrades they require.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act passed 62-33 on Nov. 19, with support from both parties. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no. The bill now heads to the Republican-controlled House of Representatives, where its future is uncertain and the legislative window is shrinking.

What the bill would do

The more than 400-page bill, led by Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah alongside Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, would shorten deadlines for many federal environmental reviews, narrow the window to sue developers over certain environmental concerns, and restrict the circumstances under which approvals for projects can be withdrawn.

It would also bar grid operators from shifting the incremental costs of serving data centers onto other customers, regardless of a facility's size — a ratepayer protection written into the bill after lawmakers raised concerns that households and small businesses were being left to pay for the power infrastructure new data centers need.

An analysis from the Rhodium Group, an independent research firm, estimated the bill would reduce household electricity bills by between $50 and $78 a year by 2040. The bill also bolsters clean energy sources such as wind and solar, and it was endorsed by President Donald Trump.

The objections

Environmental advocates and Native American tribal groups opposed the bill, saying it would weaken bedrock environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act, and could infringe on treaty rights and endanger sacred sites. Hawley said the bill was "stuffed with giveaways to data centers and industry at the expense of farmers."

Sen. Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat who voted for the bill, said it was "not perfect" and that he was disappointed that his amendments to improve its environmental and historic preservation provisions failed, but called it "an important step forward to lower costs for American families."

What it means here

Webb County has been weighing data-center proposals and the power demands that come with them, and residents have raised questions about who pays when the grid has to grow. If the House passes the Senate bill, federal reviews for power plants, transmission lines and data centers would move faster, and developers — not neighboring ratepayers — would have to cover the transmission costs their projects create. That trade is the heart of the debate now moving to the House: speed and lower bills on one side, weaker environmental review and tribal protections on the other.
